questions.topic: What a stateful inspection adds over a packet filter
questions.learningObjective: Explain what stateful inspection adds over a packet filter
questions.stem: A team believes its firewall is stateful because it tracks sessions for network address translation. What does a stateful inspection add over a packet filter?

options.text: It tracks the state of each connection, so return traffic is judged against the connection it belongs to
It examines the payload of every packet, so threats inside the body are caught
options.misconception: believes stateful inspection means payload inspection

options.text: It resolves names for each packet, so spoofed destinations are dropped before routing
options.misconception: attributes name resolution to a stateful firewall

options.text: It encrypts traffic between sites, so inspection happens inside the tunnel
options.misconception: confuses state tracking with tunnel encryption

questions.explanation: A packet filter judges each packet on its headers, while a stateful device remembers which connections exist and admits return traffic because it belongs to an established flow. Tracking translation alone does not give that.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a permit rule for return traffic assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the assumptions behind a blanket return-traffic permit rule
questions.stem: Explain what a permit rule that allows any return traffic for an allowed connection quietly assumes about the traffic it admits.

answer.exemplar: The rule grants permission to the response side of a flow without asking anything further about it, so it assumes the response can only travel back to the originator, that the originator is the machine the flow began with, and that nothing else can be made to look like that reply. Each of those assumptions can fail when addresses are reused, when a device is compromised, or when a forged packet carries the right identifiers and arrives on the permitted path.

questions.explanation: Such a rule grants permission on the basis of an earlier decision, so it assumes the reply belongs to that conversation and cannot be forged. Addresses are reused and hosts are compromised, so both assumptions can fail.
questions.hint: Think about what the rule never checks.

options.misconception: applies the proportion to the whole instead of the relevant subset

options.text: 8,000 sessions, one in four of the 32,000 sessions on port 443
2,400 sessions, the share taken from the 9,600 sessions on port 21
options.misconception: uses the blocked service's count as the basis

options.text: 1,600 sessions, found by applying one in four to the 6,400 mail sessions
options.misconception: applies the rate to the wrong port's sessions

questions.explanation: Only the 32,000 sessions on port 443 carry payloads the rule cannot inspect, and one in four of them is 8,000. Applying the rate to the whole 48,000 would count ports whose contents the rule does see.

questions.topic: What micro-segmentation adds over one coarse zone

stimulus.body: The organisation runs one flat internal zone that contains the payment gateway, the staff laptops and the building management controllers. A proposal exists to split the zone so that each class of device has its own policy.

questions.stem: The estate runs one flat internal zone. What would micro-segmentation add that the single zone cannot provide?

options.text: Higher throughput between the workstation pool and the payment gateway
options.misconception: expects segmentation to improve internal throughput

options.text: A single policy that covers every internal device with one set of rules

options.text: Separate policies per device class, so one compromised device does not expose the rest
Automatic failover between the payment gateway and the building controllers

questions.explanation: One zone forces a single decision on every internal device, so a compromised workstation put the payment gateway offline. Separate policies per device class contain the blast radius without isolating everything at once.
questions.hint: Think about what one zone must decide at once.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a switch port limit on learned addresses really counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a learned-address port limit actually counts
questions.stem: Explain what a switch port limit on learned addresses actually counts and why that is not the same as limiting the number of devices attached.

answer.exemplar: The limit counts source addresses the switch has seen arriving on that port, so it is a bound on how many distinct senders the port has heard from, not on how many physical devices are plugged in. A single device that sources traffic from several addresses, or a virtual machine that presents a different address, consumes several of the permitted slots. Conversely several devices sharing one address occupy a single slot, so the limit can be reached by one sender or by one address with several machines behind it.

questions.explanation: The limit is on distinct learned source addresses on that port, so one device presenting several addresses or one address behind several machines behaves differently from the simple case. It bounds addresses seen, not cables plugged in.
questions.hint: Think about what the switch records per port.

options.misconception: invents a long lived subset the scenario never mentions

questions.hint: Divide the refusals by all connections seen.

options.misconception: suggests trusting tunnelled content the gateway cannot inspect

options.text: The state check is limited; it cannot judge the inner flow's state at all

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What micro-segmentation adds over one coarse zone
questions.learningObjective: Explain how micro-segmentation narrows the blast radius
questions.stem: Explain why micro-segmentation changes the blast radius of a compromised device rather than merely adding another policy to the existing estate.

answer.exemplar: A coarse zone forces one decision to cover every device in it, so the moment one host is untrustworthy the whole group must be treated the same way, which is why an entire payment service goes offline to contain a single laptop. With micro-segmentation the policies are written per group, so the workstation loses its own access while the payment gateway keeps running with a policy that never depended on that workstation. Containment becomes selective instead of absolute, and the operational cost of an incident falls with it.

questions.explanation: One zone makes every device share a fate, so isolating one means isolating all. Per-group policies let the affected device lose access while the rest keep their own policy, which makes containment selective rather than absolute.
questions.hint: Think about what a single zone must decide together.

questions.topic: What a virtual LAN boundary does not isolate
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a dual-attached device defeats a virtual LAN boundary

stimulus.body: Two virtual LANs share a switch, and the team treats the split as a security boundary. The switch configuration was unchanged throughout.

options.text: The boundary was crossed by a device that was legitimately attached to both sides
The switch configuration was wrong, so the virtual LANs should be rebuilt
options.misconception: blames the switch for traffic from a legitimate port

options.misconception: assumes the boundary was bypassed inside the switch fabric

options.text: The two devices from sending frames to one another across that shared port

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a virtual LAN boundary does not isolate
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a virtual LAN split is not a security boundary
questions.stem: Explain why a virtual LAN split inside one switch should not be described to the business as a security boundary.

answer.exemplar: The split keeps unicast and broadcast traffic inside its own virtual LAN, but every device on the switch still shares the physical port, the switch's own control plane and any uplink the site provides. A host that is dual attached, or one that is compromised, sits inside the boundary while also reaching beyond it, so the separation is a way of organising traffic rather than a way of confining an attacker. Only routing and firewalling between the two provides that confinement.

questions.explanation: The split organises traffic inside the switch, but devices on it remain able to reach beyond the boundary, so it does not confine an attacker. Confinement comes from routing and filtering between the two virtual LANs.
questions.hint: Think about what devices on the switch can still reach.

questions.topic: What a private virtual LAN prevents on a shared port
questions.learningObjective: Explain the local scope of private virtual LAN privacy
questions.stem: Explain why a private virtual LAN on a shared port does not protect a device from traffic arriving from anywhere else on the switch.

answer.exemplar: The arrangement separates the two devices attached to that one port from each other, because the switch will not forward a frame between their private virtual LANs. It says nothing about the rest of the switch, and any frame that arrives on another port is delivered according to that port's own virtual LAN membership. The device still receives ordinary traffic, and it can still be reached by anything on the switch that shares its addressing, so the privacy is local to the port rather than a property of the device.

questions.explanation: The private virtual LAN separates the two attached devices from each other only. Frames from other ports are still delivered according to their own virtual LAN membership, so the device is not shielded from the wider switch.
questions.hint: Think about where the other frames come from.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an access list cannot inspect in the header it matches
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a header-only access list is bypassed by the far end
questions.stem: Explain why an access list that matches only on address and port can be fully bypassed by an attacker who controls the server behind the permitted port.

answer.exemplar: Every field the list examines is chosen by the other end of the connection or is the same for every connection to that server, so the attacker can satisfy all of them while the traffic does whatever the attacker wants. A rule of the form permit that destination on that port says nothing about which application is speaking or what it is carrying, so a permitted address that serves something else entirely passes unchallenged. The list's judgement is exhausted before it reaches the part that matters.

questions.explanation: Addresses and ports are chosen by the far end, so an attacker who controls that server can satisfy every field the list checks while sending anything at all. The rule's judgement stops short of the application and the content.
questions.hint: Think about who chooses the fields the list reads.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a switch port limit on learned addresses really counts
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of setting a low learned-address limit
questions.stem: Explain why a learned-address limit on a switch port is often set below the number of devices a team expects to attach, and what that trade is buying.

answer.exemplar: The limit is a bound on the number of distinct senders the switch will learn from one port, and setting it low means the port will not silently accommodate a large or changing population of addresses, which is the behaviour of a router or hub being plugged into the access network rather than an endpoint. The cost is that legitimate devices are refused, and the benefit is that the port cannot become a convenient place to attach something the access network was never meant to carry.

questions.explanation: Setting the limit low keeps the port behaving like an access port rather than a shared segment, so it cannot silently accept a large changing population of addresses. The cost is that legitimate extra devices are refused.
questions.hint: Think about what a low limit prevents being attached.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a permit rule for return traffic assumes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a return-traffic rule depends on bounded state
questions.stem: Explain why a permit rule for return traffic is usually paired with a limit on the state table that holds the connections it depends on.

answer.exemplar: The rule can only admit a reply because the gateway remembers the flow it belongs to, so the rule's protection and its risk both sit in that table. Every open flow consumes an entry, and a table that fills up makes the gateway forget flows, which it then treats as unknown and refuses, or worse, admits under a looser fallback. Bounding the table therefore bounds how long a half-open flow can linger and how many replies the rule can legitimately allow at once.

questions.explanation: The rule's ability to admit a reply depends entirely on the remembered flow, so the table holds both the protection and the risk. A table that fills causes the gateway to lose track of flows, which it must then treat as unknown.
questions.hint: Think about where the rule keeps what it relies on.

questions.hint: Compute the remainder, then divide by the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a virtual LAN boundary does not isolate
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to describe a virtual LAN split accurately
questions.stem: Explain what a team should say about a virtual LAN split when a business case presents it as a security control.

answer.exemplar: The honest description is that the split keeps layer two traffic inside its own virtual LAN and forces anything crossing between them through a routing device, which is where a policy can be applied. It is not a boundary in its own right, because a device attached to the switch, or one holding an address on both sides, is not contained by it. Presenting it as the control rather than as the enabler of the control misstates what the estate will actually get.

questions.explanation: The split keeps layer two traffic in its own virtual LAN and forces crossings through a router, so it enables a policy rather than being one. It does not contain a device that is attached to the switch or holds addresses on both sides.
questions.hint: Think about how the split should be described.

questions.topic: What an access list cannot inspect in the header it matches
questions.learningObjective: Explain the gain and the remaining limit of application matching
questions.stem: Explain why adding an application name to an access list's match fields improves its usefulness without making it a complete control.

answer.exemplar: Matching on the application name lets the rule express the policy the business actually has, because the port alone hides which service is really speaking on it. It is still a decision made on one header field chosen by the other end of the connection, so anyone who can influence that field can still satisfy the rule, and the rule still says nothing about the content once the application is running. It is a meaningful improvement and not a complete answer.

questions.explanation: Matching on the application name lets the rule express the real policy rather than a port guess, which is a genuine gain. It remains one field chosen by the far end, so it can still be influenced and it still says nothing about content.
questions.hint: Think about what the new field gives and what it leaves.

questions.topic: What a private virtual LAN prevents on a shared port
questions.learningObjective: Explain the asymmetry of private virtual LAN protection
questions.stem: A private virtual LAN on a shared port keeps the two attached devices from seeing each other, yet the rest of the network reaches them as before. Explain why that asymmetry exists.

answer.exemplar: The switch delivers a frame to a port according to the virtual LAN membership the frame carries, and the private virtual LAN arrangement makes the two attached devices share no virtual LAN in which their traffic could meet. That is a property of the relationship between those two devices on that one port. Frames from any other port travel in their own virtual LAN and are delivered exactly as before, so the arrangement does not alter what the rest of the network can reach, and neither does it stop a device from being attacked from elsewhere.

questions.stem: An access list matches on destination address and destination port. Which change would most improve the rule's ability to enforce the business's application policy?

options.text: Matching on the source address instead of the destination address
options.misconception: moves the blind spot to another header field

options.text: Adding the source port to the fields the rule already matches on
options.misconception: adds a field that does not describe the application

options.text: Matching on the application name as well as on the address and port
Adding the packet's time of arrival to the fields the rule matches on
options.misconception: adds a field that carries no policy meaning

questions.explanation: The application name is the field that reflects which service is actually speaking, so adding it lets the rule express the policy the business has. Source addresses, source ports and arrival times describe the connection's shape rather than its application.
questions.hint: Ask which field names the service in use.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a private virtual LAN prevents on a shared port
questions.learningObjective: Compute the address demand of adding a private virtual LAN to a port
questions.stem: A shared port carries 3 private virtual LANs, and each private virtual LAN currently presents 2 addresses. The port's learned-address limit is 6. If one more private virtual LAN were added with the same 2 addresses each, how many addresses would the port then be trying to learn?
questions.explanation: The three private virtual LANs already present six addresses, and adding a fourth with two more makes eight the port would need to learn. That is two addresses beyond the limit of six, so the port would stop learning and raise a violation.
questions.hint: Multiply the virtual LANs by the addresses each one uses.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a stateful inspection adds over a packet filter
questions.learningObjective: Explain why stateful devices expose a resource a filter does not
questions.stem: Explain why a stateful gateway is harder to exhaust than a packet filter that only makes allow or deny decisions on each packet.

answer.exemplar: A packet filter answers each packet in isolation, so an attacker whose traffic simply matches an allowed rule is never made to wait and never consumes anything beyond the cost of the check. A stateful gateway accepts a flow, then spends an entry in its table to remember it, so the number of concurrent flows is a resource the attacker can consume, and once the table is full the gateway must refuse or forget. The stateful device therefore offers a place to apply a limit that a stateless filter simply does not have.

questions.explanation: A stateless filter makes no record, so allowed traffic costs nothing beyond the check itself. A stateful gateway must spend a table entry per flow, which gives an attacker something to exhaust and gives the defender somewhere to apply a limit.
questions.hint: Think about what each device must remember.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an access list cannot inspect in the header it matches
questions.learningObjective: Compute the number of rules blind to the application distinction
questions.stem: A site access list has 20 rule lines, of which 3 match on the application name. If the list enforced the same policy on a host that could reach every permitted destination directly, how many rule lines would still be unable to distinguish two applications on one port?
questions.explanation: Only the 3 lines that match on the application name can tell two applications apart, so 17 of the 20 lines remain blind to that difference. Removing the other fields from the rule changes nothing about the fact that they read the same headers.
questions.hint: Subtract the application-matching lines from the total.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What an access list cannot inspect in the header it matches
questions.learningObjective: Judge the effect of adding an application match to an access list
questions.stem: The site's access list matches on destination address and port, and a new rule has been proposed that also matches the application name. Which judgement about that proposal is best supported?

options.text: The list is adequate; the new rule should be rejected as unnecessary complexity
options.misconception: dismisses a real improvement to coverage as complexity

options.text: The list is inadequate; it should be replaced by a stateful firewall instead
options.misconception: jumps to another control without weighing the narrow change

options.text: The list is limited; the new rule narrows the blind spot without closing it
The list is limited; the new rule makes the list a complete control
options.misconception: claims one extra field removes every blind spot

questions.explanation: The rule reads only headers, so it cannot tell which application is speaking. Adding the application name narrows that blind spot without closing it, since the far end still chooses the matched value.
questions.hint: Ask what the new field still leaves unexamined.
